Before we look at the code, remember why we manipulate it. In our last lesson, we saw how Recombinant DNA turns bacteria into medicine factories.

Key Concepts:

Remember

Synthetic hormones match human ones, reducing allergic reaction risks compared to animal-derived versions.

screens.title: How do we actually read the code?
screens.html:
How do we actually read the code?

Imagine trying to fix a complex machine without a manual. That was genetics before the 1970s.

We knew DNA held the instructions, but we couldn't read the specific order of As, Cs, Gs, and Ts. DNA sequencing changed everything. If you could read your own genetic code, what would you want to find out first?

screens.title: KEY CONCEPT
screens.html:
KEY CONCEPT

The Sanger Method: The Gold Standard

Developed by Frederick Sanger in 1977, this method uses 'chain termination'.

It relies on interrupting DNA replication at specific points to determine the sequence. This discovery earned Sanger his second Nobel Prize.

screens.title: The Secret Weapon: ddNTPs
screens.html:
The Secret Weapon: ddNTPs

Normal DNA building blocks (dNTPs) have an -OH group for chain extension. Sanger used dideoxynucleotides (ddNTPs), which act as 'stop' signals because they lack this group.

Normal dNTP

Contains the 3' hydroxyl group needed for nucleotide bonding.

Dideoxy ddNTP

Lacks the 3' hydroxyl group, causing DNA polymerase to stop.

screens.title: The Sequencing Reaction
screens.html:
🔍

The Sequencing Reaction

A sequencing reaction contains:

Template DNA

DNA Polymerase

Primers

Plenty of normal dNTPs

A small amount of fluorescently labelled ddNTPs (one colour for each base).

Example

If a ddATP (red) is incorporated, the chain stops at an adenine.

screens.title: Step-by-Step: Chain Termination
screens.html:
Step-by-Step: Chain Termination

Denaturation

The double-stranded DNA is heated to separate into single strands.

Primer Annealing

A short primer attaches to the start of the target sequence.

Extension

Polymerase builds the strand until a random ddNTP terminates it.

screens.title: Using Electrophoresis to Read
screens.html:
🔑

Using Electrophoresis to Read

After the reaction, we have thousands of fragments of different lengths. We separate them using Capillary Electrophoresis.

Smaller fragments move faster. As they pass a laser, the fluorescent tag is read.

Key point

The sequence is read from the shortest fragment (the one closest to the primer) to the longest.

screens.title: The Electropherogram
screens.html:
The Electropherogram

The computer translates the laser signals into an electropherogram — a graph with peaks.

Each peak represents a specific nucleotide. By reading the peaks in order, we get the DNA sequence.

screens.title: HISTORY
screens.html:
HISTORY

The Human Genome Project (HGP)

Started in 1990, the HGP was a 13-year international effort to sequence all 3.2 billion base pairs of the human genome.

It was the largest collaborative biological project in history, involving thousands of scientists worldwide.

screens.title: Goals of the HGP
screens.html:
Goals of the HGP

Identify all of the approximately 20,000–25,000 genes in human DNA.

Determine the sequences of the chemical base pairs that make up DNA.

Store this information in public databases for researchers.

Address the ethical, legal, and social issues (ELSI) arising from the project.

screens.title: What is DNA Mapping?
screens.html:
What is DNA Mapping?

Sequencing tells us the order of bases; Mapping tells us where genes are located on specific chromosomes.

Think of sequencing as reading the words in a book and mapping as creating the index that tells you which page the chapters are on.

screens.title: Application: Personalized Medicine
screens.html:
🔍

Application: Personalized Medicine

Genome mapping allows doctors to see if you have specific mutations that make you more likely to respond to a certain drug.

This is called Pharmacogenomics — the right drug, at the right dose, for the right person.

Example

The BRAC1 and BRAC2 gene mutations can indicate a significantly higher risk of breast cancer.

screens.title: Detecting Genetic Disorders
screens.html:
Detecting Genetic Disorders

Sequencing is used to diagnose rare diseases that standard tests miss.

We can identify single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) — minute variations that might cause conditions like Cystic Fibrosis or Sickle Cell Anaemia.

screens.title: DISCUSSION
screens.html:
DISCUSSION

Ethics: Genetic Privacy

Who should own your genetic data? If an insurance company finds out you have a 'bad' gene, can they charge you more?

In Australia, the Genetic Information Non-discrimination debate is ongoing. There are fears that genomic data could lead to a new form of social stratification.

screens.title: The 'Right Not to Know'
screens.html:
The 'Right Not to Know'

If you are sequenced for one condition, and researchers find you have a gene for an incurable disease (like Huntington's), should they tell you?

This raises questions of autonomy and psychological harm. Some people would rather live without the 'genetic sword of Damocles' hanging over them.

screens.title: Commercial Genomic Testing
screens.html:
Commercial Genomic Testing

Companies like 23andMe allow you to send a spit sample and receive your ancestry and health risks.

However, these are often not as accurate as clinical tests and may lack the professional genetic counselling needed to interpret scary results.

screens.title: Future Frontiers: CRISPR
screens.html:
Future Frontiers: CRISPR

Once we map and sequence the genome, the next step is editing it. CRISPR-Cas9 is a tool that allows for precise changes to the DNA sequence.

We will explore this in detail in upcoming lessons. It turns sequencing from a 'read-only' process into 'read-write'.

screens.title: Summary of DNA Sequencing
screens.html:
Summary of DNA Sequencing

1

Preparation & Termination - DNA is amplified, mixed with dNTPs/ddNTPs, and fragmented.

2

Separation & Analysis - Electrophoresis sorts fragments; lasers read fluorescent tags.

screens.html:
Final Reflection

If you were offered a full genome sequence for free, would you take it? What would be the biggest benefit and the biggest risk to you personally?

Risk: Stress from incurable conditions/Privacy concerns regarding data.

questions.title: Written practice
questions.prompt: Distinguish DNA sequencing from genetic mapping and describe one use of sequence comparison.
steps: Sequencing determines the order of nucleotide bases in a DNA region.
Genetic mapping locates genes or markers relative to one another, for example using recombination data.
Comparison of homologous DNA can identify variants or help infer evolutionary relationships, using appropriate evidence and methods.

o: Only the length of an entire organism
bank.why: Sequencing identifies the order of bases in a DNA molecule or region.

bank.q: What does a genetic map describe?
o: Relative positions of genes or markers
The amino acid sequence of every protein
bank.why: Genetic maps describe relative positions and can use recombination frequencies.

o: To identify similarities and differences that inform relatedness
To prove every difference is adaptive
To eliminate the need for other evidence
To determine age from any base alone
bank.why: Sequence comparisons can inform evolutionary relationships when interpreted with suitable methods and other evidence.
